title: Self-custody vs. collaborative custody vs. exchange
premise: Bitcoin's properties, savings that can't be inflated and payments that can't be censored, only hold if you are the bearer. A custodian reintroduces the counterparty risk Bitcoin exists to remove, links your identity to your holdings, and makes you a named target for a wrench attack you didn't need to invite. Everything below assumes this as the starting point, not something up for debate.
question: What accountability are you actually taking on with full self-custody, versus collaborative custody (a co-signing service or third party holds one key in a multisig with you), versus leaving funds on an exchange? What did each option let you avoid, and what did it cost you?
framing: One live position, offered to be tested here rather than assumed: collaborative custody is “abdication-as-a-service”. You are still trusting someone else's solvency, honesty, and continued willingness to cooperate, just with better branding than an exchange. Is that fair, or does collaborative custody solve a real problem (loss of a single key, no heir with technical skill) that pure self-custody doesn't?

title: Should you roll your own entropy?
question: A hardware device's TRNG can generate a seed for you in seconds. Rolling your own entropy (dice, shuffled cards) takes longer and requires you to trust your own procedure instead of a chip. What does rolling your own actually buy you, and what does skipping it cost you?
framing: Framing to test, not to assume: for the entropy step specifically, there's no way to verify a non-deterministic output after the fact. You can only control its source in the first place. If that's right, generating it yourself may be the only point in the whole setup where “verify, don't trust” isn't actually possible, and controlling the source is the only lever available. Is that framing correct, or is there a way to gain assurance about a device's TRNG that doesn't reduce to trust?
